articles.title: Berkeley Homes proposed 1,060 homes in later phases of a London scheme and cut the development’s overall affordable-housing commitment from 40% to 12%; councillors unanimously rejected the revision
articles.summary: Members of Southwark Council's planning committee have unanimously rejected revised plans from housebuilder Berkeley Homes for the Bermondsey Place
articles.body: Members of Southwark Council's planning committee have unanimously rejected revised plans from housebuilder Berkeley Homes for the Bermondsey Place development on the Old Kent Road. The decision came after the company reduced its affordable housing offer from 40 per cent to just 12 per cent. Local councillors voted against the plans despite their own planning officers recommending approval. Their decision showed strong opposition to the sharp cut in affordable homes in a major regeneration area in south London. According to reports published by Southwark News, The Architects' Journal, and MyLondon, the revised plans covered 1,060 homes across the second and third phases of the wider development. Under the new proposal, just 81 of these 1,060 homes would have been affordable, a major drop from the original promise made for the site.Viability challenges behind the reductionThe original combined planning permission for Bermondsey Place was approved in 2020. It allowed around 1,300 homes to be built across three phases, with a firm commitment that 40 per cent of the entire development, measured by the number of rooms suitable for living, would be affordable housing. Phase 1 includes 285 homes and is currently being built. It still follows the original promise of providing 40 per cent affordable housing. However, when Berkeley Homes submitted new plans for the remaining phases, the company argued that rising construction costs and changing economic conditions had made the original target too expensive to deliver. As explained by legal and planning website Planning Geek, the developer proposed a new design prepared by architecture firm PRP. The changes included different building heights and sizes, revised building layouts, and changes to public spaces. The plans also added second staircases to meet updated building safety rules. Under the company's revised financial calculations, keeping the original 40 per cent affordable housing in Phase 1 while reducing the figure to 12 per cent in Phases 2 and 3 would have brought the total affordable housing across the entire development down to just 17.9 per cent. To address this reduction, Berkeley Homes proposed three separate reviews of the project's financial position during construction. These reviews would allow the council to secure more affordable housing contributions if market conditions improved.Council committee takes firm stanceAlthough planning officers advised that the reduced offer was the highest level of affordable housing the project could currently afford, members of Southwark Council's planning committee rejected the application in a unanimous 6-0 vote. During the meeting, councillors raised concerns about the long period planned for completing the homes. They also questioned the financial figures and assumptions provided by the developer. Comments from council leaders showed strong frustration with efforts to reduce the amount of social and intermediate housing in the development. Speaking to MyLondon, Councillor Victor Chamberlain, Deputy Leader of Southwark Council and Executive Member for Neighbourhoods, Strategic Planning and Wellbeing, praised the committee for refusing to accept the developer's proposed cuts. "It's vital that new development in Southwark brings what local people and communities badly need, especially much-needed affordable housing," Chamberlain said in statements reported by MyLondon. "Both these planning applications seek to do the opposite and cut the amount of affordable housing, so we have refused them both." Chamberlain also said he would write formally to the Mayor of London. He wanted City Hall to respect the council's decision rather than step in and overturn the local refusal.Developer defends scheme and points to council feesBerkeley Homes expressed strong disappointment with the committee's decision to reject the plans despite the recommendation from its own professional planning officers. The company pointed to additional costs and building regulations as major reasons for the project's financial difficulties. Justin Tibaldi, Managing Director at Berkeley Homes, defended the company's position in statements given to MyLondon. He highlighted the large financial contributions that local authorities were requiring from the development. "We are disappointed that the committee overruled its own planning officers' recommendation and blocked over 1,000 new homes and hundreds of jobs within a designated regeneration area," Tibaldi said. "We are particularly concerned that members would not acknowledge or engage with the council's own analysis of the site's viability challenge." Tibaldi also argued that charges imposed by the council were reducing the money available to support affordable housing on the site. "The decision also fails to recognise that the council is charging this project £30 million through its Community Infrastructure Levy and Section 106 requirements, which is funding that could otherwise be used to increase the number of affordable homes," Tibaldi stated. He added that Berkeley Homes remained committed to the development and was considering what steps to take next.Wider battle over London housing targetsThe dispute over Bermondsey Place reflects a wider disagreement across London. Local councils are trying to meet affordable housing targets, while housebuilders are dealing with inflation, rising material costs, and new fire safety requirements. The rejection also comes as Southwark Council continues to push back against developers who want to change their existing planning commitments. As reported by MyLondon, London's Mayor, Sadiq Khan, has considered taking control of planning decisions in the borough when local refusals could delay the delivery of overall housing targets. For Bermondsey Place, the rejection means there is now uncertainty over when the remaining 1,060 homes will be built. articles.title: In 2003, a New York mother transferred property to her son and daughter-in-law after he promised to return it when asked; 23 years later, an appeals court upheld cancellation of the deed when they refused to give it back
articles.summary: A New York appeals court on Wednesday upheld a ruling cancelling a 2003 property transfer after a mother, Josephine Catalano, took legal action against
articles.body: A New York appeals court on Wednesday upheld a ruling cancelling a 2003 property transfer after a mother, Josephine Catalano, took legal action against her son and daughter-in-law for refusing to return her property in Rockland County. Josephine had transferred ownership to the couple after her son verbally promised to give it back whenever she asked. More than two decades later, the court ruled in her favour, finding that she had relied on her son's promise when transferring the property.According to the ruling, Josephine Catalano had transferred the property, located in Rockland County, New York, to her son, Carmine D. Catalano Jr., and his wife, Denise Catalano, in 2003. However, she had kept the right to use the property during her lifetime. According to court records, Josephine agreed to transfer ownership because Carmine had verbally assured her that he would return it whenever she wanted.Although the property was legally transferred to her son and daughter-in-law, she maintained that the understanding between them was that she could ask for it back. The promise was not written into the property deed, but she said it was the reason she had agreed to the transfer.The disagreement arose when Josephine eventually asked the couple to return the property. They refused, prompting her to take legal action. She asked the court to cancel the 2003 deed and restore her rights over the property.Mother takes son and daughter-in-law to courtJosephine approached a court in Rockland County, arguing that her son had failed to honour the understanding on which she had transferred the property.She wanted the court to recognise that the couple should not be allowed to keep ownership after refusing to fulfil the promise that had led her to transfer it in the first place.The court heard the case without a jury, meaning a judge examined the evidence and decided the outcome. On November 21, 2024, the judge ruled in Josephine's favour. The court found that she had provided strong and convincing evidence showing that the property had been transferred because of her son's promise.The judge ordered a legal remedy known as a constructive trust which meant the couple could not continue holding the property for their own benefit when the circumstances of the transfer required it to be returned to Josephine.The court also cancelled the original 2003 deed and rejected the claims Carmine and Denise had made against Josephine. However, the couple did not accept the decision and challenged it before a higher court.Appeals court examines son's promiseThe case then reached the Appellate Division, Second Department, where judges reviewed the evidence and the earlier ruling.The central question was whether Josephine had shown that her son made a promise, that she relied on it when transferring the property and that the couple's refusal to return it was unfair. The judges found that the evidence supported her account.They agreed with the lower court that Carmine had promised to transfer ownership back to his mother whenever she requested it. They also accepted that Josephine had relied on this assurance when she signed the property over to him and his wife.The judges also noted that the trial judge had heard the witnesses directly and was therefore in a better position to assess their credibility. After reviewing the findings, they saw no reason to overturn the earlier decision.Court rejects couple's argumentsCarmine and Denise raised several objections to the earlier ruling. One concerned Denise's ownership rights. The couple argued against applying the court's order to her share of the property. However, the appeals court found that her ownership could also be covered by the order requiring the property to be held for Josephine's benefit.The couple also questioned whether a verbal promise could be used to challenge a formal property transfer. Property transactions generally involve written documents, and the defendants relied on legal rules concerning written agreements and evidence to challenge Josephine's case.However, the appeals court found that those rules did not prevent the lower court from acting on Carmine's verbal promise in these circumstances. The judges also agreed with the decision to reject the couple's claims against Josephine.The appeals court thus upheld the cancellation of the October 2003 deed and the order protecting Josephine's interest in the property. It also awarded her legal costs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Will you comply with Japanese laws? Japan plans new question for foreign visitors on entry form
articles.summary: Japan is considering introducing a new question on its immigration entry form that would require foreign nationals arriving in the country to declare
articles.body: Japan is considering introducing a new question on its immigration entry form that would require foreign nationals arriving in the country to declare whether they intend to follow Japanese laws and regulations.The proposed change, put forward by Japan's Immigration Services Agency, would require foreign nationals applying for permission to land in Japan to answer: "Are you willing to comply with Japanese laws and regulations?"The proposal is part of a draft amendment to a Justice Ministry ordinance. The agency opened a public consultation on October 29, with submissions accepted until November 27, 2026.Under the existing rules, foreign nationals applying to enter Japan must submit an entry record form to an immigration inspector. The document collects basic information, including the traveller's name, date of birth and purpose of visit, along with other details required for immigration screening.The proposed amendment would add a new fourth item to the form, with a heading referring to the applicant's willingness to comply with Japanese laws and regulations.The agency has also proposed revisions to two other immigration-related forms, although the draft does not specify the precise changes to those documents.Why Japan wants to introduce the new questionThe Immigration Services Agency said the number of foreign visitors to Japan has been increasing. It acknowledged that only some foreign nationals have been involved in behaviour that allegedly violates Japanese laws and rules, but said such conduct had prompted concerns.Against this backdrop, the agency believes it is appropriate to confirm whether foreign nationals intend to follow Japanese laws at the stage when they apply for permission to land in the country.The agency said the information would be considered as part of the landing examination before a decision is made on whether to allow an individual to enter Japan.However, the draft documents do not explain how an applicant's answer would be assessed or whether answering negatively would automatically lead to refusal of entry.When could the new rule take effect?Japan plans to finalize and promulgate the ministerial ordinance in December 2026, with the proposed changes scheduled to take effect in January 2027.These dates are currently proposed timelines and are not yet final.The public consultation opened on October 29 and will remain open until November 27. Individuals and organizations can submit their opinions through Japan's e-Gov portal, by email or by post to the Immigration Services Agency.Submissions must be made in Japanese and include reasons supporting the comments. The agency has said it will not respond individually to people who submit their views.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Six US governors and 21 city mayors host landmark Diwali celebrations across Pacific Northwest
articles.summary: In one of the largest-ever Diwali celebrations across the US Pacific Northwest, six state governors and mayors from 21 cities have joined hands with the
articles.body: In one of the largest-ever Diwali celebrations across the US Pacific Northwest, six state governors and mayors from 21 cities have joined hands with the Indian-American community to host special ceremonies marking the festival of lights at governors’ mansions, state capitols and city halls.Governors of Idaho, Nebraska, Montana, North Dakota and Washington have hosted first-of-their-kind Diwali celebrations at their respective governors’ mansions and state capitol rotundas, attended by US Senators, members of the US Congress, local mayors and prominent Indian-American community leaders. The celebrations, which began in mid-October, will culminate on 10 November, when the Governor of Oregon is scheduled to host the final ceremony at the State Capitol in Salem.The unprecedented celebrations have also provided an opportunity for state leadership to acknowledge the significant contributions of Indian Americans to their respective states, particularly in strengthening local economies, enriching cultural diversity and fostering community engagement.Several governors used the occasions to underline the importance of the Indian-American community and its growing role in the social, economic and civic life of their states.At the Idaho State Capitol on October 16, Governor Brad Little said, “Here in Idaho, we’re proud to have a vibrant Indian community that contributes very much to our state through their businesses, professions, service and civic involvement. Indian Americans help strengthen Idaho’s economy and help our communities be better places to live, work and raise a family.”Speaking at the Nebraska Governor’s Mansion in Lincoln on October 20, Governor Jim Pillen described the Indian community as “an incredibly vital piece of who we are as the people of Nebraska”, urging families to preserve their cultural traditions. “It’s really important that you keep these traditions alive in your families. Never, ever, ever let the light go out!” he said.At the Governor’s Residence in Bismarck on October 29, North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong highlighted the enduring ties between the two communities, saying: “We should celebrate these relationships. We should celebrate these friendships. Diversity is our strength...” He added that the partnership would continue to grow across international, trade, state-to-state and diplomatic engagements, but, above all, at the human level.Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, addressing the gathering at the State Capitol Rotunda in Olympia on Wednesday, highlighted the remarkable growth of the Indian-American population in the state and its contributions. “We are proud to be home to one of the largest shares of Indian Americans in the country. And during the previous decade, we had the fastest growing Indian American population in the entire country. And we have seen this community contribute so much to our state,” he said.The celebrations have extended well beyond state capitals. In Washington State, 21 cities across the Greater Seattle region, home to nearly 200,000 Indian Americans, have also organised individual Diwali ceremonies in their respective City Council chambers. Presided over by city mayors, the events have featured traditional lamp-lighting ceremonies attended by members of the city councils.The participating cities include Auburn, Everett, Marysville, Kirkland, Bellevue, Tukwila, Medina, Bothell, SeaTac, DuPont, Spokane, Issaquah, Edmonds, Lynnwood, Duvall, Tacoma, Mukilteo and Kent. Further ceremonies are scheduled in the coming days in Snoqualmie, King County, which encompasses 39 cities in the Greater Seattle area, and the City of Seattle, all on 10 November.Adding to the significance of the celebrations, several state and city governments have issued official proclamations recognising Diwali as a festival symbolising the triumph of light over darkness. The proclamations also acknowledge the Indian-American community’s contributions to the economic and cultural enrichment of their regions and reaffirm the continuing partnership with the Consulate General of India in Seattle.The celebrations build on an important legislative milestone in Washington State, where the State Senate passed Senate Bill 6044 in February 2026, recognising Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas as state observances, though not as legal public holidays.The Consulate General of India in Seattle has worked closely with Indian-American community leaders across the six states and the participating cities to organise and co-host the large-scale celebrations.You use AI every day. articles.title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Washington State Democratic Party calls girls' sports initiative unconstitutional
articles.summary: Shasti Conrad, Washington State Democratic Party chair, calls voter-approved girls' sports Initiative 638 unconstitutional and backs court challenges.
articles.body: Washington State Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad called a voter-approved girls’ sports measure unconstitutional and said the party would support groups seeking to challenge it in court. "While this result is incredibly disheartening, voters in Washington and across the nation rejected anti-trans candidates up and down the ballot," Conrad said in the Nov. 5 statement. "The fight over I-638 is just beginning. We believe this initiative is unconstitutional on its face and support organizations planning to challenge it in court." The Washington State Democratic Party sent a statement to OutKick stating, "WA Dems will not be challenging the initiative in court. We believe there will be organizations who do and we support those efforts." WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS The party also declined to make Conrad available for an interview. Voters approved Initiative 638, which bars students the measure defines as biologically male from competing in girls’ K-12 athletic competitions. It also requires students seeking to compete in female-only sports to submit a health examination form or other statement from a health care provider verifying their biological sex based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels. The Associated Press called the measure as passed, with about 56.6% support in results reported by Axios. The measure does not specify which examinations or tests providers must use. Opponents have warned it could lead to invasive exams or testing for girls. Let’s Go Washington, the group behind the initiative, says providers can rely on existing medical records and that the measure does not require genital exams. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has said its current sports physical rules do not require genital, DNA or hormone testing. Conrad said the measure "undoes protections in Washington state law passed 20 years ago" and added, "To every trans girl participating in school sports, please know that we support your right to play." I-638 changes Washington’s longstanding policy allowing students to participate on teams consistent with their gender identity. WASHINGTON STATE'S HIGH SCHOOL SPORTS LEAGUE PUTS ONUS FOR TRANS ATHLETE CONTROVERSY ON STATE LAWS The statement also highlighted voters’ rejection of two other measures backed by Let’s Go Washington: I-001, concerning parental rights and access to student information, and I-645, which sought to repeal the state’s new tax on income above $1 million, which has nothing to do with girls' sports. Voters approved I-638, the third measure in the group’s 2026 ballot effort. The Gender Justice League said it was evaluating legal options, while the ACLU of Washington declined to discuss potential litigation. I-638 is set to take effect Dec. 3, pending certification of the election results. Conrad’s statement also pointed to Jaelynn Scott’s election to the state House. Scott is set to become Washington’s first openly transgender state legislator and the first out Black transgender woman elected to a state legislature in the country. Here are three insert-ready paragraphs on the Washington cases: The dispute became especially visible in Camas, where about a dozen girls on the high school cross-country team walked off before a race to protest a transgender teammate’s participation. The runner had competed in the boys’ category earlier in the season before switching to the girls’ team; the district and the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association said her participation complied with existing rules. Washington’s wrestling policy is also being challenged in federal court. A Puyallup student identified in court filings as K.M.K. alleges that a transgender opponent sexually assaulted her during a December 2025 girls’ match. The claim has not resulted in criminal charges. K.M.K.’s family sued state and school officials and has asked the Supreme Court for emergency relief after lower courts denied an injunction. The Supreme Court docket showed the application remained pending as of its latest listed filing on Nov. 3. A girls’ basketball game in Tumwater prompted a separate Title IX dispute. In February 2025, Tumwater player Frances Staudt sat out a game against Shelton after learning a transgender student was on the opposing girls’ team. A complaint filed on Staudt’s behalf alleged that the district denied her a fair opportunity to compete and retaliated against her for speaking out. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The U.S. Department of Education opened an investigation; that action was an inquiry into the allegations, not a finding that the district violated Title IX. Tumwater said it took the matter seriously and would work with the department.

articles.title: India’s only floating post office gets longer working hours
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Working hours at India’s only Floating Post Office, operating from a houseboat on Dal Lake in Srinagar, have been extended from five hours to 12
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Working hours at India’s only Floating Post Office, operating from a houseboat on Dal Lake in Srinagar, have been extended from five hours to 12 hours, Department of Posts announced Friday. According to the revised timings, the post office (PO) at Nehru Park will now remain open from 9am to 9pm.The move follows increased footfall and public demand for postal services beyond regular office hours, chief postmaster general, Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, Col Sagar Hanuman Singh said during a visit to the facility. He reviewed arrangements and interacted with locals and tourists.Col Singh said the initiative aims to provide greater convenience to customers. The extended hours will provide locals, houseboat operators, and tourists greater flexibility to access postal services, officials said.In 1953, the PO operated from a simple postal boat, catering to communities living on Dal Lake. It served as a vital link between the houseboats and the city. In 2011, the facility was officially renamed the Floating Post Office—an idea John Samuel, then-postmaster general of the J&K circle, introduced.The PO has a unique museum of rare stamps and postcards that portray the history of the postal service in J&K. Over time, it has become a popular tourist attraction.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Idaho man says he paid the entire price for a property bought with his partner; Supreme Court overturns ruling giving her 50% ownership after their breakup
articles.summary: An Idaho man who says he paid the entire purchase price and covered every expense of a property bought with his former partner has been caught up in a
articles.body: An Idaho man who says he paid the entire purchase price and covered every expense of a property bought with his former partner has been caught up in a legal battle over its ownership. After their relationship ended in 2020, his former partner transferred her interest in the property to a California nonprofit organisation, only for it to be transferred back to her several weeks later. The dispute reached the Idaho Supreme Court, which overturned a lower court's decision awarding the woman a 50 per cent share and ordering the property to be sold. The case has now been sent back for further proceedings.Who paid for the Idaho property before the couple's breakupPaul Martin Bedell and Joanne Parsons were in a romantic relationship between 2007 and 2020. They were never married and lived together for much of their relationship at Parsons' home in California. According to the Idaho Supreme Court judgment, Bedell contributed towards the utilities, maintenance and other household expenses while living there, but did not pay rent or a mortgage. The couple also testified that they jointly purchased investment properties in California to renovate and resell for profit.In 2014, Bedell and Parsons purchased a property in Bonneville County, Idaho. Both their names appeared on the purchase and sale agreement and the special warranty deed filed in the county. Bedell paid the property's taxes, utilities, insurance and other expenses. Parsons testified that they had purchased it as a vacation home and jointly hosted family members and friends there. Bedell subsequently maintained that he had paid the entire purchase price.Why did Parsons transfer her property share to a California nonprofitBedell and Parsons ended their relationship in 2020. Following the separation, Bedell made the Idaho property his primary residence. Parsons subsequently transferred her interest in the property to a nonprofit organisation in California through a quitclaim deed. Several weeks later, the nonprofit transferred the interest back to Parsons, also through a quitclaim deed.Bedell then filed a lawsuit in Bonneville County, seeking a declaration that Parsons had no ownership interest in the property and requesting that the title be placed solely in his name. He later amended his complaint to include a partition claim, asking the court to award him the entire property. Parsons filed a counterclaim seeking a declaration that she held a 50 per cent ownership interest and requesting that the property title be held jointly in both their names.Why did the court award Parsons 50% ownership of the Idaho propertyThe ownership dispute was considered alongside an earlier Idaho Supreme Court decision, Demoney-Hendrickson v. Larsen, issued in 2023. That ruling established a rebuttable presumption of equal ownership when two individuals' names appear on a warranty deed without specifying their respective interests. The presumption can be challenged through evidence demonstrating that the parties intended a different ownership arrangement.Relying on this principle, the district court concluded that Parsons held a 50 per cent interest in the property. It found that Bedell had not provided sufficient evidence to overcome the presumption of equal ownership and ordered a partition by sale. The court also considered evidence presented by Parsons, including her claims that she participated in selecting the property, helped negotiate its purchase price, decorated its interior and provided materials for an outbuilding. Bedell disputed several of these claims.Why did the Idaho Court overturn the 50% property ownership rulingBedell challenged the district court's decision, arguing that it had failed to properly consider his evidence. He presented testimony and other records to support his position that he had paid the entire purchase price, covered the property's expenses and never intended to give Parsons an ownership interest. He also disputed her account of her financial and other contributions towards the property.The Idaho Supreme Court agreed that the evidence raised genuine disputes of material fact that could not be resolved through summary judgment. It explained that the district court had improperly weighed the parties' conflicting evidence and assessed their credibility at that stage of the proceedings. The judgment stated: "Those disputes should have been resolved at trial, not on summary judgment." The justices also clarified that having someone's name on a warranty deed does not necessarily mean that person must hold an ownership interest greater than zero.The Supreme Court reversed the decision granting Parsons summary judgment on the ownership dispute, the denial of Bedell's request for reconsideration and the award of costs and attorney fees to Parsons. However, it clarified that it had not concluded that Bedell had successfully overcome the presumption of equal ownership. It had only determined that his evidence was sufficient to establish a genuine dispute requiring further proceedings.The court also upheld the district court's separate decision that Bedell had waived any claim for contribution because he had not included it in his original or amended complaint. The case was remanded to the district court for further proceedings, leaving the former couple's respective ownership interests unresolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Prince Harry and five others seek to challenge Mail publisher privacy ruling
articles.summary: The Duke of Sussex and other public figures lost a High Court case against the publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday.
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex and five other high-profile figures who lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday are seeking to challenge the High Court ruling.

Prince Harry, singer Sir Elton John and actress Elizabeth Hurley were among the group facing paying joint legal costs of up to £34.5m after the court ruled in July they had failed to prove the allegations of unlawful information gathering.

Associated Newspapers Limited strongly denied the claims, which were heard at an 11-week trial in London that ended with judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissing all the allegations.

At the time, a spokesperson for the publisher described the judgement as an "overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists".

The prince testified in person during the civil hearing and claimed the details that appeared in 14 articles about him "plainly" proved journalists were listening in to phone calls - but a High Court judge said he had failed to prove that .

On Friday, a spokesperson for Prince Harry, Hurley, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish, actress Sadie Frost and political campaigner Baroness Lawrence said the claimants had filed applications with the Court of Appeal applying for permission to challenge the judgements.

The statement said the planned appeal was both on Mr Justice Nicklin's dismissal of their claims and a subsequent indemnity costs order.

The spokesperson said: "The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed."

In August, a month on from his judgement, Mr Justice Nicklin ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before the trial .

He also ordered at that time the claimants should make an initial payment of £9.54m while the final total was calculated.

The statement from the group's joint spokesperson did not make any reference to Liberal Democrat politician Sir Simon Hughes who was part of the action. The BBC has contacted Sir Simon to establish whether he is joining the appeal.

After the costs ruling, he told the BBC he was "disappointed" and would take "the time necessary to consider both the substantive and the costs judgment and whether to pursue appeals against decisions in either judgment or both".

The trial saw many current and former Mail and Mail on Sunday journalists and executives giving evidence denying accusations of illegal activity that was put to them by lawyers representing the prince and his fellow claimants.

Lawyers for the publisher said in court that the journalists had provided a "compelling account of a pattern of legitimate sourcing of articles", including using information provided by friends and "leaky" social circles surrounding those they had written about.

In a civil case such as this, the legal convention is that the losing party must reimburse "reasonable" legal fees incurred by the other side. They also have to settle their own legal costs.

articles.title: In 1980, Stephen King bought a red Victorian home in Maine for $135,000; 46 years later, the house holds his literary archives while a neighbouring mansion offers writers 10-day residencies and $2,500 stipends
articles.summary: Forty-six years after Stephen King bought a red Victorian mansion in Bangor, Maine, for $135,000, the famous property has officially become a centre for
articles.body: Forty-six years after Stephen King bought a red Victorian mansion in Bangor, Maine, for $135,000, the famous property has officially become a centre for literary research and a place where working writers can focus on their work. The dark red Second Empire house at 47 West Broadway is well known for its unusual wrought-iron gate decorated with bats and webbed gargoyles. It now holds King's large collection of literary archives. Next door, the historic Brown Mansion operates as a fully funded writers' retreat. Selected writers can stay for 10 days and receive a $2,500 stipend. According to official information published by The Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation, the non-profit organisation founded by the bestselling author and his wife, the two projects give selected writers dedicated time to write, comfortable accommodation, and financial support. They also help preserve the historic neighbourhood.Historic home transformed for literary preservationKing and his wife, Tabitha, bought the house, which was built in 1858, in 1980 for $135,000. For more than four decades, the former home of a wealthy timber businessman served as the couple's main family residence. It also provided creative inspiration for the fictional town of Derry, Maine, which appears in novels such as It and Insomnia. In late 2019, the Bangor City Council unanimously approved the Kings' request to change the zoning of their 3.27-acre property. The land was changed from a single-family residential zone to a contract zone. This allowed the couple to turn their home into a non-profit archive centre and officially establish the neighbouring guest house as a writers' retreat. Under the city-approved plan, King's private papers, original manuscripts, and personal literary materials are kept inside the main red mansion. The archives are not open to the general public as a tourist attraction or museum. However, scholars, researchers, and literary experts can visit by making an appointment.Structured residencies with financial supportThe nearby Second Empire building at 39 West Broadway, known as the Brown Mansion, is home to the foundation's writers' residency programme. The foundation offers 10-day stays that give small groups of writers a quiet place to work and a chance to connect with the local community. Writers staying at the mansion receive private bedrooms and bathrooms, shared living areas, a fully stocked kitchen, and group dinners every evening. To make sure that money does not prevent writers from taking part, the foundation gives each participant a $2,500 payment. This can be used for travel costs or other personal expenses.According to the application guidelines on the foundation's official website, the retreat focuses on different groups of writers each year:Recent MFA graduates: This category is open to writers who completed a graduate degree in creative writing, fiction, non-fiction, poetry, playwriting, or screenwriting within the previous three years.K-12 educators: This category is open to full-time primary and secondary school teachers. Retired teachers with at least eight years of classroom experience can also apply.Maine writers: This category is for people who currently live in Maine or grew up in the state. Applicants must have a record of published books or contributions to literary journals.Applications are judged based on the quality of the writing samples and the proposed work plans. The selection process is anonymous, meaning reviewers do not know the applicants' identities.Preserving neighbourhood character while supporting artistsThe decision to turn the private home into an archive centre and writers' retreat was intended to protect the historic property for the future while preventing large numbers of tourists from visiting the residential area. During the original zoning approval process, city officials and lawyers representing the Kings stressed that the retreat would operate quietly and respect the people living nearby. Speaking to The Bangor Daily News, planning officials explained that the non-profit arrangement would help protect an important city landmark while preserving the peaceful character of West Broadway. By bringing King's personal literary archives together with fully funded writers' stays next door, The Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation has kept the historic property closely connected to the art of storytelling.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay starting 12-day Latin America tour
articles.summary: The 71-year-old pontiff is visiting three countries despite undergoing surgery to remove a tumour last month.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay as he begins a 12-day tour of South America, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.

The 71-year-old head of the Roman Catholic Church touched down in Montevideo on Friday after a 13-hour flight from Rome, telling reporters he feels “fairly good”.

“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place,” Leo told reporters on board the papal plane. “I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward. And I am very happy to say praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I’m here today, I think in fairly good shape.”

On his trip, the pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades.

His packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay – the region’s least Catholic and most secular country – will include a visit to a neighbourhood with heavy gang violence, a mass in Paysandu, about 375 kilometres (230 miles) from Montevideo, and another mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometres (60 miles) from the capital.

Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, told the AFP news agency that there was “widespread interest in the pope’s visit that goes well beyond the confines of the Catholic Church”, with tickets for masses in Paysandu and Florida quickly running out.

The regional trip is somewhat of a homecoming journey for Leo, as he will finish in Peru in three weeks, where he served for almost two decades as a missionary, forming a deep attachment to the continent.

The trip will take the pope to the former Inca capital of Cusco and the Amazon rainforest, and he will also revisit his old diocese of Chiclayo for a private visit to a chapel he helped rebuild.

Leo said on Wednesday that he was looking forward to returning to a region “so dear to me”.

The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said he hoped the trip would “strengthen faith, renew hope, and rekindle the fire of charity” in the countries he is visiting, which face rising inequality and violence, as well as a decline in Catholic followers.

Despite undergoing an operation on October 13 to remove a cancerous tumour , doctors have given him the all-clear to travel, and the Vatican said no special medical measures were necessary beyond the standard care on papal trips.

“His stamina is fantastic. The way that he’s singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief. She noted that Leo had passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his surgery and was eager to get on the road.

articles.title: One popular fruit may support brain and heart health as you age, experts say
articles.summary: Harvard researcher Walter Willett eats blueberries almost daily for heart and brain health. Here's what studies say about the polyphenol-rich fruit.
articles.body: A cup of blueberries can give your breakfast a boost and experts say it may also support heart and brain health. Walter Willett, an 81-year-old Harvard nutrition researcher known for decades of work on diet and chronic disease, recently told The Washington Post that he eats blueberries almost every day, usually adding them to oatmeal with Greek yogurt and nuts. "In study after study, berries appear to be protective against neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease," Willett told the outlet. "It's an area where we need more research, but berries do seem to stand out, especially blueberries." NATURAL COMPOUND IN BLUEBERRIES AND GRAPES MAY UNLOCK FAT-BURNING PROCESS IN MUSCLE CELLS The fruit is one of the most researched, along with apples, bananas and citrus fruits, according to experts, and studies have long examined blueberries' effects on blood vessels and cognition. In a six-month study of 115 adults with metabolic syndrome, participants who consumed the equivalent of about a cup of blueberries daily showed improvements in blood-vessel function and arterial stiffness, Dr. Nadim Geloo, Virginia-based senior medical director of Abbott's structural heart division, told Fox News Digital. POPULAR FOOD COULD BOOST HEART HEALTH, BUT THE AMOUNT YOU NEED TO EAT MAY SURPRISE YOU That doesn't mean they directly prevent heart attacks or strokes, however. "Most [studies] small and short, often use freeze-dried powder rather than whole fruit, measure markers like blood vessel function rather than actual heart attacks or strokes and are frequently funded by the blueberry industry," Geloo said. Some studies have also found improvements in memory and other cognitive measures, especially among older adults, though Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist and physician at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City, noted that those effects were modest and research has not shown blueberries can prevent Alzheimer's disease. COMMON KITCHEN STAPLE MAY SHARPEN YOUR BRAIN, AND IT ONLY TAKES 2 TABLESPOONS California-based biomedical researcher Rhonda Patrick also recently spoke about blueberries' benefits for heart and brain health on her FoundMyFitness podcast. "The strongest benefit is vascular," she said. Patrick called blueberries "one of the better-supported polyphenol-rich foods," referring to their antioxidant properties, and also said a "practical dose" is about a cup a day. THE 8 HEALTHIEST BEANS YOU SHOULD BE EATING MORE OFTEN, ACCORDING TO NUTRITION EXPERT She noted that studies in older adults have also found improvements in some measures of memory and cognitive flexibility. "While there is no 'magic bullet,' there's nothing to lose by including more berries in your diet." Longer-term observational studies have also linked berry intake with slower cognitive decline, but they cannot prove blueberries caused the difference. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Nonetheless, experts say it's still worth eating them. "While there is no 'magic bullet,' there's nothing to lose by including more berries in your diet," Elisa Bremner, a New York-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. She, too, eats them nearly every day, Bremner said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "I have heard blueberries called 'brainberries,' due to all the research on cognitive function associated with them," she said. One cup of blueberries also provides about 3.6 grams of fiber, Bremner noted, which helps slow digestion, and pairing blueberries with protein-rich foods such as yogurt may further slow the release of sugar. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Fresh and frozen blueberries are both practical options, Bremner said, noting that frozen fruit can be a convenient, lower-cost way to eat fruit year-round. Since the evidence does not show that everyone needs to eat exactly a cup daily or that blueberries can prevent disease, Bremner recommends eating a varied, balanced diet rather than relying on one fruit. articles.title: Cornell faculty vote 'no confidence' in university leadership after alleged fraternity gang rape
articles.summary: Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring "no confidence" in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep di...
articles.body:
Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring "no confidence" in the school's top leaders , a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024 .

The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.

The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman's allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.

While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.

The board of trustees said Friday that the vote reflected deep anger on campus and sent a "clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable," but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to "thoughtfully and comprehensively" address the issue.

"The Board fully supports President Kotlikoff and his administration as they continue to listen and act decisively in support of students," board chair Anne Smalling said in a statement. She cited expanded sexual assault prevention education, additional victim advocates and more staff at the university's Office of Civil Rights as evidence of the administration's response.

Thomas Giuffra, Jane Doe's attorney, said in a statement Friday that "we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.

All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.

Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write "reflection" papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.

Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.

Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.

Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution's sponsors to emphasize that "the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg" and that "a veritable fortress of silence has been breached" around sexual violence since the resolution's introduction.

Cornell's president defended his leadership

Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution , Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes.

Kotlikoff defended his leadership , arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell's reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman's case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell.

Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.

Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman's initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.

The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff's resignation.

articles.title: One more chance for excluded voters in Delhi, 6 other states
articles.summary: They won't have to fill form 6, EC says NEW DELHI: Electors across seven states/UTs undergoing SIR, including Delhi, who were excluded from the draft
articles.body: They won't have to fill form 6, EC saysNEW DELHI: Electors across seven states/UTs undergoing SIR, including Delhi, who were excluded from the draft electoral roll on account of being absent, shifted, dead or duplicate (ASDD) and whose enumeration forms (EFs) were not received, will be provided one more opportunity to get their names included in the final electoral roll by filling up the SIR form afresh. They will no longer have to fill Form 6, meant for fresh enrolment, or Form 8, if they were excluded due to shifting of place of residence within the same state/UT.The drive in states where SIR is under way - Delhi, Haryana, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland - may come as a relief for deleted electors who were reluctant to fill Form 6 to be added back, in view of the declaration in the form that they were enrolling for the first time. "Basically, the enumeration window which stopped with the publication of draft roll is being reopened for the deleted ASDD voters till the end of the claims and objections period," an EC official said.EC, in a letter to chief electoral officers of the above states/UT, said ASDD electors may submit their EF physically or online to the electoral registration officer or booth-level officer (BLO), along with an annexure mentioning the reason why they could not submit it earlier and declaring that they have not submitted Form 6 for fresh enrolment during SIR.An elector who was excluded due to shifting of residence within the same state/UT can submit the EF along with an annexure mentioning why it was not submitted earlier and declaring that they have not submitted Form 6 during SIR. In the annexure, such voters must mention the address where they were enrolled earlier as well as the address to which they have now shifted. Residence proof will need to be attached.The EF, along with the annexure, must be submitted to the ERO of the assembly constituency to which the voter has shifted. The poll panel said partially filled EFs of left-out ASDD electors will be generated afresh in the ERO dashboard in ECINet. The district election officer and ERO shall make all efforts to contact such electors through BLOs.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) Friday released date sheets for the Class X and XII board examinations for 2027, with both scheduled to begin on Feb 16.The schedules were announced 101 days before the start of the examinations, giving students more than three months to prepare.According to a circular issued by CBSE controller of examinations Sanyam Bhardwaj, over 46.3 lakh students have registered for the 2027 examinations - more than 26.5 lakh from Class X and over 19.8 lakh from Class XII. While Class X students will appear in 83 subjects, Class XII students will take examinations in 121 subjects.All examinations will begin at 10.30 am.CBSE said the date sheets were finalised after the completion of the list of candidates submission process by schools and an analysis of the subject combinations opted for by students.Explaining the scheduling process, the board said, "More than 40,000 subject combinations have been factored in while preparing the date sheets to ensure that examinations of any two subjects opted by a student do not coincide on the same date."It said adequate gaps had been provided between examinations of subjects commonly offered together in both classes. It added that the tentative schedules of major entrance tests for Class XII students were also taken into account, with efforts made to conclude the boards before the entrance tests.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Former Los Angeles sheriff's deputy tried to smuggle 1.1 pounds of heroin worth $226,000 inside two Pringles cans into California jail; accepted $16,500 in  payments; sentenced to 67 months in prison
articles.summary: A former Los Angeles County Sheriff's deputy has been sentenced to more than five years in federal prison for attempting to smuggle approximately 1.1
articles.body: A former Los Angeles County Sheriff's deputy has been sentenced to more than five years in federal prison for attempting to smuggle approximately 1.1 pounds of heroin, worth an estimated $226,000, into a California jail concealed inside two Pringles potato chip cans.According to the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Michael Meiser, 40, was sentenced to 67 months in federal prison by US District Judge Fernando M. Olguin on November 5. Meiser had pleaded guilty in July 2025 to one count of possession with intent to distribute heroin at the North County Correctional Facility in Castaic, California.Federal prosecutors said Meiser was working as a Sheriff's deputy at the facility, where he was assigned to an intelligence and investigative unit monitoring gang activity. According to the DOJ, he had agreed with inmates to smuggle narcotics into the jail in exchange for cash and payments through the Cash App digital wallet.Deputy allegedly received $16,500 for smuggling heroinAccording to the DOJ's account of the case, one of Meiser's relatives received $1,500 through Cash App on April 24, 2024, from an individual connected to an inmate. The relative subsequently informed Meiser about the payment.Six days later, on April 30, Meiser drove his BMW to a Chevron petrol station in Valencia, where he collected a plastic grocery bag from two women in a Chevrolet SUV. One of the women was associated with a jail inmate.The bag contained two Pringles cans stuffed with approximately 511 grams (1.1 pounds) of heroin. It also contained two white envelopes carrying a total of $15,000 in cash, which prosecutors identified as the remaining payment for bringing the drugs into the jail.The heroin was reportedly worth approximately $226,000 inside the correctional facility, where inmates sold the narcotic in tiny quantities known as 'papers', according to Sheriff's officials.How investigators caught the deputyAfter collecting the consignment, Meiser allegedly placed the grocery bag inside his green backpack, which also contained his loaded handgun. He then drove to a fellow Sheriff's deputy's apartment complex and joined the colleague in his truck for the journey to the correctional facility.According to the DOJ, the other deputy drove the vehicle through the jail's initial security checkpoint and parked inside the complex. Meiser then got out, took his backpack and transferred the heroin-filled Pringles cans into the trunk of a Sheriff's radio car, hiding them beneath computer towers.He subsequently removed the $15,000 in cash from the grocery bag and placed it back inside his backpack. Later that day, Meiser also met with an inmate involved in the smuggling arrangement and spoke to him for several minutes.However, as Meiser and the other deputy were leaving the facility, Sheriff's investigators stopped their vehicle.Investigators arrested Meiser and searched the deputy's truck, where they recovered the green backpack containing $15,000 in cash, Meiser's loaded handgun, badge and Sheriff's Department identification. They also searched the radio car and discovered the two Pringles cans containing heroin.The FBI investigated the case with assistance from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department's Internal Criminal Investigations Bureau. Assistant US Attorney Kathy Yu prosecuted the case, according to the DOJ.Investigation raised questions about deputy's relationship with inmatesBeyond the drug-smuggling operation, the case also brought scrutiny to Meiser's unit and its relationship with influential inmates who allegedly exercised considerable control within the correctional facility.According to an investigative report by the Sheriff's Department's Internal Criminal Investigations Bureau, which worked alongside FBI agents, the unit appeared to acknowledge that gang leaders held considerable influence over inmates, sometimes more than the jail authorities themselves.In an internal affairs review, Meiser's partner, Deputy Jose Mungui, described being 'on the same page' with inmate 'shot callers' when dealing with issues such as overdoses and violence. He reportedly told investigators that deputies felt powerless to prevent certain incidents and would sometimes approach gang leaders to request that they refrain from killing inmates or harming officers.Mungui maintained that the approach was intended to minimise chaos inside the jail. He also described Meiser as someone who had developed a rapport with several inmates.Coded phone conversations helped expose the alleged operationThe Los Angeles Times, in its report on the case, detailed how investigators began uncovering the extent of Meiser's connections with inmates in February 2024 after examining a series of suspicious jail telephone conversations.The calls involved Jose Rodriguez, a reputed gang member and alleged shot caller at the facility, and his purported right-hand man, Jackie Triplett.During one conversation, Triplett spoke to a woman who mentioned purchasing 'white Jordans' and 'black Jordans'. Investigators interpreted the phrases as coded references to methamphetamine and heroin.The following day, jail surveillance footage reportedly showed Meiser handing Triplett a bag and a bedroll. Later that night, Triplett called the woman to thank her, and she reportedly told him it was his 'time to shine', according to the investigative report cited by the newspaper.Two months later, investigators recorded another conversation in which an inmate from Rodriguez's housing unit read out a sequence of numbers. The numbers were subsequently decoded as a request for Pringles, investigators said.The following day, internal affairs detectives obtained a warrant to install a tracking device on Meiser's BMW. Investigators subsequently followed him to the Chevron petrol station in Valencia, where he collected the grocery bag containing the heroin.No other deputies implicated in the smuggling schemeAlthough the case brought considerable scrutiny to Meiser's unit and its dealings with inmates, no other deputies have been implicated in the drug-smuggling operation.The investigation exposed how Meiser allegedly exploited his position as a law enforcement officer and his access to a correctional facility to facilitate the attempted distribution of a substantial quantity of heroin.Meiser has now been sentenced to 67 months in federal prison following his guilty plea, bringing the federal prosecution to a significant conclusion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle appears in court over child sex abuse material
articles.summary: The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented.
articles.body:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

Markle was arrested on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.

The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for almost 20 years.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".

Markle's court hearing lasted for 30 minutes, and the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

He was brought into court a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.

The court ordered Markle to submit to home detention at his assisted living facility in Florida and electronic monitoring.

No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.

FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.

"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.

He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".

Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.

In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.

The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.

The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.

In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.
